source: Graber, Franklin, Gordon (2005) Diagnostic error in internal medicine, Arch Intern Med 165:1493-1499
finding: 100 cases of diagnostic error in internal medicine were analysed. Cognitive causes were present in most. This is the founding quantitative result for the subfield.
numbers: 100 cases kept from 129 suspected (29 excluded); sources: quality-assurance reviews, voluntary reports, autopsy discrepancies. 90 cases had patient injury, 33 deaths (abstract). Cognitive factors in 74 cases (74%), 320 instances in total (about 4.3 per cognitive case, my division). System-related factors in 65% (228 instances). Mixed 46%, cognitive only 28%, system only 19%. No-fault factors in 44 cases, sole cause in 7.
limits: Non-random, voluntary cases from internal medicine only. No interrater statistic; consensus by team. Hindsight bias in retrospective review. Root-cause assignment subjective.
agent_relevance: Errors are mostly in reasoning steps, not lack of facts, and they stack (about 4 per case). A scaffold should expect several small slips per failed case, not one big one.

source: Graber, Franklin, Gordon (2005) Diagnostic error in internal medicine, Arch Intern Med 165:1493-1499 - breakdown of cognitive errors
finding: Faulty synthesis dominated the cognitive errors. Faulty knowledge was rare. Premature closure was the single most common named cognitive factor.
numbers: Faulty synthesis about 264 instances (Table 2 subheads 159 information processing + 106 verification = 265; one-count discrepancy in the paper). Faulty data gathering 45. Faulty knowledge or skills only 11 (4 knowledge, 7 skills). Premature closure 39 (about 12% of 320 cognitive instances, my division).
limits: Premature closure is counted inside the verification group, so it overlaps faulty synthesis. Categories were set by the authors.
agent_relevance: Knowledge deficit is a small share (11 of 320). The failure is in combining and checking evidence. This supports code-checked verification (G2, G3) over more knowledge or more reasoning text.

source: Graber, Franklin, Gordon (2005) Diagnostic error in internal medicine, Arch Intern Med 165:1493-1499 - what was missed
finding: The paper gives no table of missed diagnoses by condition. Pulmonary embolism appears only as an example (bronchitis called, PE found later).
numbers: Condition-level counts: none reported in the paper.
limits: Do not cite Graber 2005 for 'common diseases are missed most'. Use Schiff 2009 (a04) for condition counts.
agent_relevance: Keep the claim 'mostly missed common diseases' marked as only partly supported.

source: Schiff et al. (2009) Diagnostic error in medicine: analysis of 583 physician-reported errors, Arch Intern Med 169:1881-1887
finding: Clinician-reported missed or delayed diagnoses, coded by process step. Most errors were in testing, then in assessment (failure to consider or overweighing a competing diagnosis).
numbers: 669 cases from 310 clinicians at 22 institutions; 583 kept. Severity: 162 major (28%), 241 moderate (41%), 180 minor (31%). Top missed: pulmonary embolism 26 (4.5%), drug reaction/overdose 26 (4.5%), lung cancer 23 (3.9%), colorectal cancer 19 (3.3%), acute coronary syndrome 18 (3.1%), breast cancer 18 (3.1%), stroke 15 (2.6%). Phase: testing 44%, clinician assessment 32%, history 10%, exam 10%, referral 3%.
limits: Abstract read only. Self-reported, convenience sample from grand rounds; recall bias; no denominator of all cases.
agent_relevance: Assessment errors (32%) are the reasoning part. Failing to order or follow up a test (44%) is a process gap that code can enforce with an open-test list that blocks closure.

source: Singh, Meyer, Thomas (2014) The frequency of diagnostic errors in outpatient care, BMJ Qual Saf 23:727-731
finding: Population-level estimate of how often outpatient diagnosis fails.
numbers: Combined estimate 5.08% of US adult outpatients per year, about 12 million adults; about half possibly harmful. Built from three studies (two electronic-trigger studies, primary care and colorectal cancer follow-up; one lung cancer series).
limits: Abstract read only. Extrapolation from chart-review studies with trigger tools; not a direct audit of all visits.
agent_relevance: Base rate: failure is uncommon per case but large in total. Doubt should not fire on every case (G1); it needs a signal.

source: Mamede, Schmidt, Rikers et al. (2008) Effects of reflective practice on the accuracy of medical diagnoses, Med Educ 42:468-475
finding: Reflective reasoning helped only for complex cases. For simple cases it made no difference.
numbers: 42 internal medicine residents, Brazil, 16 cases; interaction case complexity x reasoning mode F(1,41)=4.48, p<.05. No main effect of reflection.
limits: Abstract read only. Small sample, instruction manipulation; one country.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for any reflection step: gate it on difficulty, not on every case (supports G12).

source: Mamede, van Gog, van den Berge, Rikers, van Saase, van Guldener, Schmidt (2010) Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents, JAMA 304:1198-1203
finding: The central experiment that induces a bias in doctors. Recent similar cases pulled second-year residents to the earlier diagnosis. Structured reflection recovered accuracy.
numbers: 18 first-year and 18 second-year residents. Phase 1: 6 cases evaluated; phase 2: 8 new cases solved by nonanalytical reasoning, 4 resembling earlier cases with a different diagnosis; phase 3: those 4 redone by reflection. Second-years scored 1.55 (CI 1.15-1.96) on similar cases vs 2.19 (CI 1.73-2.66) on others, p=.03 (max 4.0). First-years showed the reverse: 2.03 vs 1.42, p=.046. Second-years gave the phase-1 diagnosis 1.44 times vs 0.72 times per resident, p=.04. Reflection raised similar-case scores to 2.03 (second-years) and 2.31 (first-years), p=.006.
limits: Abstract read only. 36 participants, one centre, one bias (availability). No control group redoing the cases without reflection, so a practice effect is not ruled out. The first-year reversal is unexplained.
agent_relevance: An earlier similar case in context biased the next one. This mirrors leftover context from earlier attempts, so it supports a fresh context per attempt (S3). The reflection was a structured reanalysis of findings, not 'think again'.

source: Norman, Sherbino, Dore, Monteiro et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of system 1 versus system 2 reasoning, Acad Med 89:277-284
finding: Telling doctors to slow down and be thorough did not raise accuracy. This tests the idea that bias comes from fast thinking.
numbers: Second-year residents, 3 Canadian schools: n=96 (2010, speed instruction) and n=108 (2011, reflect instruction); 20 computer cases. Accuracy 44.5% vs 45.0%, not significant. Time 69 s vs 89 s per case, p<.001. Wrong cases took 17 s longer on average.
quote: simply encouraging slowing down and increasing attention to analytical thinking is insufficient to increase diagnostic accuracy
limits: Abstract read only. Two different year cohorts, not randomised within one year. Instruction effect only; no structured method tested.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the 4b row 'telling the model to slow down'. Also, wrong cases take longer, so long deliberation signals trouble, not care.

source: Norman, Monteiro, Sherbino, Ilgen, Schmidt, Mamede (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning: cognitive biases, knowledge deficits, and dual process thinking, Acad Med 92:23-30
finding: Review that questions the bias account. Errors come from both fast and slow thinking. Knowledge deficits matter. Bias awareness teaching does not cut errors.
numbers: Qualitative review, no pooled number in the abstract. Biases can be induced experimentally (availability best shown) but their share of real errors is not well established. Knowledge-reorganisation strategies give small but consistent benefit.
quote: Educational strategies directed at the recognition of biases are ineffective in reducing errors
limits: Abstract read only. Narrative review by authors who hold a view that competes with the Croskerry school.
agent_relevance: Backs 4b (bias checklists do not work). Warning: the schema should not name 'bias' as the cause; it should test the specific failure with a check.

source: Croskerry (2003) The importance of cognitive errors in diagnosis and strategies to minimize them, Acad Med 78:775-780
finding: Founding catalogue paper. Names 'cognitive dispositions to respond' (CDRs): perception failures, failed heuristics and biases. Proposes metacognition and cognitive debiasing as the cure.
numbers: Qualitative. The paper lists many CDRs (anchoring, premature closure, availability and others) and strategies. No trial data in the abstract.
limits: Abstract read only (full text fetch redirected). The CDR list is an expert catalogue, not tested for predictive validity. Its call for debiasing was later largely not supported (a08, a09).
agent_relevance: Source of the field's bias vocabulary. Use the catalogue to design checks, not as a prompt checklist (4b).

source: Berner & Graber (2008) Overconfidence as a cause of diagnostic error in medicine, Am J Med 121(5 Suppl):S2-S23
finding: Review: physicians underestimate the chance their diagnosis is wrong. This feeds early stopping.
numbers: Qualitative in the abstract; covers incidence of error, evidence on overconfidence and strategies.
limits: Abstract read only. Calibration numbers not read. See the Calibration and overconfidence subfield.
agent_relevance: Link to the calibration subfield. Supports 4b: do not stop on stated confidence.

source: Gupta, Harrod, Quinn et al. (2018) Mind the overlap: how system problems contribute to cognitive failure and diagnostic errors, Diagnosis 5:151-156
finding: Ethnography suggesting that system pressure and handoffs raise anchoring and premature closure in practice.
numbers: Focused ethnography, 10 inpatient teams, 286 hours (Jan 2016 to Apr 2017), 31 residents/interns in focus groups, 10 attendings interviewed, two academic centres. Cites a retrospective study of 93 errors with nearly 6 factors per case, almost half both system and cognitive. One resident paged 120 times in 24 h. Anchoring and premature closure said to rise around handoffs.
limits: Hypothesis-generating; no confirmed errors measured; two sites; self-report.
agent_relevance: Passing a conclusion from one stage to the next is where anchoring enters. Pass raw evidence, not the earlier verdict (S3).

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974) Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases, Science 185:1124-1131
finding: Founding anchoring experiment. People adjust too little from a starting number, even a random one.
numbers: From memory, not opened this session: wheel-of-fortune anchor 10 gave median 25% for the share of African countries in the UN; anchor 65 gave 45%. Verify before citing.
limits: Not opened. Later work shows anchoring is robust but its size varies with anchor type and expertise.
agent_relevance: Root of the clinical 'anchoring' label. The LLM studies (a16, a17) reuse the paradigm with hints.

source: Lieder, Griffiths, Huys, Goodman (2018) The anchoring bias reflects rational use of cognitive resources, Psychon Bull Rev 25:322-349
finding: Resource-rational account: adjustment from an anchor stops when more steps cost more than they gain, so early stopping is rational for the thinker's budget.
numbers: From memory, not opened; no numbers recorded. Verify before citing.
limits: Not opened. Fits lab estimation tasks; not tested on clinical diagnosis.
agent_relevance: A formal model of 'stop too early'. For an agent it suggests stopping rules that depend on the cost of the next check and the value of information, set in code.

source: Voytovich, Rippey, Suffredini (1985) Premature closure in diagnostic reasoning, J Med Educ 60:302-307
finding: Early clinical use of the term premature closure: accepting a diagnosis before it is fully verified.
numbers: From memory, not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Details unverified.
agent_relevance: Origin of the term. Our code can define premature closure operationally: a final answer issued while a listed alternative has no discriminating check done.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster), arXiv 2403.00811
finding: Tests anchoring, status quo, framing, group attribution and primacy in LLMs on admission decisions, and compares mitigation prompts. Not medical, but a close controlled debiasing test.
numbers: Models: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-2 7B and 13B. 400 prompts per experiment. Self-help (model rewrites its own biased prompt) left 0% biased parts for group attribution and 2.7% for framing in GPT-4. GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under framing. Awareness prompting helped some biases only; table cells were garbled in text extraction.
limits: Admissions task, not medicine. Per-cell numbers not reliably readable from the PDF; use for direction only. 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: Awareness prompts give partial gain. Self-help works by rewriting the input, which is an input hygiene step (S1). Supports 4b.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study, arXiv 2412.06593
finding: GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 are pulled by numeric anchors in the prompt. Simple fixes did not remove the pull.
numbers: 62 questions with three hint types (low anchor, high anchor, expert hint); 8 questions with an irrelevant first hint as control. Anchoring index for GPT-4 about 0.45 vs 0.61 in the human study the dataset came from. Chain of thought, thoughts-of-principles, ignore-the-anchor and reflection did not effectively reduce bias on expert-anchor questions. Giving hints from several angles (both-anchor) helped on some items.
limits: Estimation questions about daily life, not diagnosis. Small set, t-tests. Index comparison to humans is across studies.
agent_relevance: Strong match to 4b. Telling the model to ignore the anchor or reflect fails; changing the evidence it sees (several independent hints) helps. Hide any earlier verdict (G5, S3).

source: Schmidgall, Harris, Essien et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models, arXiv 2402.08113 (npj Digit Med)
finding: BiasMedQA: 1,273 USMLE questions rewritten to carry seven clinical biases. All six LLMs lost accuracy. GPT-4 was most resilient.
numbers: Models: GPT-4, Mixtral-8x7B, GPT-3.5, PaLM-2 (text-bison), Llama 2 70B-chat, PMC Llama 13B. Biases: self-diagnosis, recency, confirmation, frequency, cultural, status quo, false consensus. Authors report drops of 10 to 26 points depending on model. GPT-4 no bias 0.727; false consensus 0.625, recency 0.679, status quo 0.679, cultural 0.681, self-diagnosis 0.698. Mixtral 0.518 to 0.428 (false consensus). GPT-3.5 0.429 to 0.213. PaLM-2 0.357 to 0.139. With a bias-education prompt GPT-4 recovered nearly all (self-diagnosis 0.728, status quo 0.725); weaker models only partly.
limits: USMLE multiple choice, not open diagnosis. Anchoring and premature closure are not among the seven biases. Bias is injected as an added sentence. Table text garbled in extraction, so read the GPT-4 and Mixtral rows with care. Authors call mitigation gains modest.
agent_relevance: Education prompts help strong models and fail on weak ones, so they are not a general fix (4b). Risk is mostly for small or cheap models.

source: Nori, Daswani, Kelly, Lundberg, Ribeiro, Wilson et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models (SDBench, MAI-DxO), arXiv 2506.22405
finding: Benchmark built to expose premature closure and anchoring in LLMs: the model must request information step by step and decide when to stop.
numbers: 304 NEJM clinicopathological cases. Physicians (median 12 years) 20% accuracy at $2,963 per case. GPT-4o 49.3% at $2,745. o3 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO (o3) 79.9% at $2,397, or 85.5% at $7,184 in max-accuracy mode. Variants: Instant Answer, Question-Only, Budgeted, Ensemble.
limits: Hard NEJM cases, not common diseases. Physicians had no outside resources. Gatekeeper is itself a model. Microsoft authors; not independently replicated here.
agent_relevance: A usable test bed for early stopping. Compare stop-at-once vs stop-after-checks on the same cases.

source: Nori et al. (2025) - MAI-DxO design
finding: MAI-DxO is one model playing five personas in a loop, including Dr. Hypothesis (tracks the differential) and Dr. Challenger (argues against the leader). The paper says this is meant to mitigate individual cognitive biases.
numbers: Five roles; gains generalise across OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek and Llama families (abstract). I found no ablation isolating the Challenger's effect on closure.
limits: Design claim, not a tested mechanism for bias. Persona panels conflict with G4 if used as voters; here they are roles in one loop.
agent_relevance: Keep the explicit hypothesis list and a stop rule. Test the challenger role against a code-built counterexample search before adopting.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making, Nature Medicine
finding: LLMs on real hospital records (MIMIC-IV) did worse than clinicians at open diagnosis and followed guidelines poorly.
numbers: From memory, not opened: about 2,400 patients, four abdominal conditions. Accuracy figures not recorded; verify before citing.
limits: Not opened; the nature.com fetch redirected to a login page.
agent_relevance: Open-world stepwise diagnosis is much harder than vignettes; closure errors show up there, not on multiple choice.

source: Redelmeier & Shafir (1995) Medical decision making in situations that offer multiple alternatives, JAMA 273:302-305
finding: More options led doctors to choose neither: a close relative of default and closure effects.
numbers: Family physicians (n=287, 77% response): drug prescribed 53% with two medications to choose from vs 72% with one. Neurologists and neurosurgeons n=352 (84%). Legislators n=41 (32%).
limits: Abstract read only. Treatment choice, not diagnosis; mailed vignettes.
agent_relevance: Extra alternatives can freeze a decision. Cap the differential list and force a next test.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) - re-deciding after seeing all cases
finding: When models could change earlier anchored decisions after seeing everything, Llama models changed many.
numbers: Llama models changed 40 to 52% of decisions (Table 4); GPT-4 changed few.
limits: Admissions domain; Table 4 only partly readable.
agent_relevance: A weak model that re-decides flips many answers. Let code compare before and after; accept change only on new evidence (G2).

source: Schmidgall 2024 vs Lou & Sun 2024: model strength and bias
finding: Stronger models lose less in BiasMedQA but are more consistently anchored by numeric hints. The two results point in opposite directions.
numbers: Schmidgall: GPT-4 loses 2 to 10 points, PaLM-2 about 22 (0.357 to 0.139). Lou & Sun: 9 of 11 non-significant anchoring exceptions came from GPT-3.5.
limits: Different tasks and bias types; not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a stronger model is immune. Test anchoring on the actual model and task.

source: Mamede 2010, Norman 2014, Norman 2017 taken together
finding: Structured reflection on specific findings helped (Mamede 2010). General exhortation to be careful did not (Norman 2014). Teaching bias names did not (Norman 2017).
numbers: Mamede 2010 reflection 2.03 and 2.31 on similar cases; Norman 2014 44.5% vs 45.0%.
limits: Cross-study comparison, different populations and measures.
agent_relevance: Ask for a structured reanalysis of named findings that code lists, never a generic 'reconsider'.
